task: A strategically located border city that serves as the primary gateway for trade between two rival powers has petitioned for expanded self-governance. The city's merchant council argues that its unique position requires flexibility in tariffs, legal codes, and diplomatic representation that a distant central government cannot provide. Granting autonomy would likely increase trade revenue and reduce administrative burden, but it would also create a precedent that other prosperous cities might follow, potentially eroding central authority. The rival power has signalled that it would view the city's autonomy as an opportunity to expand its own influence there. Design a governance framework for the border city that grants sufficient flexibility to maximise its economic function while preserving its political loyalty and preventing foreign co-option.

dispatches.responsibility: Draft the master charter of autonomy: define scope of self-governance, sunset and renewal clauses, the escalation hierarchy between merchant council and central court, and the integrated adjustment cycle linking all domain offices into one coherent skeleton.

Design the fiscal framework: bounded tariff authority with numeric ceilings, revenue-sharing formula favoring the central treasury, trade-tax schedules, and automatic tripwires against debt accumulation or asset transfer to foreign creditors.

Delineate legal jurisdiction: which commercial, contract, and customs codes the city may amend locally versus which must remain central (treason, national security, foreign relations); design the dual-court structure and appeals ladder to central justice.

Establish the security architecture: central garrison independent of city command, city watch size and armament caps, border-defense chain of command, and militia restrictions to prevent any armed body becoming a vector for foreign influence.

Define diplomatic representation boundaries: permitted trade missions, merchant-host protocols, and cultural engagement; prohibited acts (treaties, military understandings); foreign-merchant registration and expulsion triggers.

Design the personnel framework: central appointment and rotation of the city's senior officials, loyalty-vetting standards, and formal advisory (non-binding) status of the merchant council on security-sensitive matters.

Construct the oversight and tripwire system: audit cadences, numeric review thresholds (trade revenue deviation, foreign debt ratio, garrison strength, diplomatic contact frequency), veto-and-reject powers, and automatic central-intervention triggers spanning every domain above.
